newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Growth in Internet use slows in Malaysia.
newsitem.headline: Growth in Internet use slows in Malaysia.

text.p: After growing 22 percent a month in 1995, use of the Internet is only expanding about five percent a month now in Malaysia, with users voicing concern over the higher cost of local phone calls, a survey said on Wednesday. The Malaysian Institute of Microelectronic Systems (MIMOS), the country's key Internet service provider, commissioned the survey.

"This year we are seeing a flattening for Internet growth in Malaysia...to about five percent a month. We think this is going to be the stable rate of growth," Mohamed Awang-Lah, vice president of MIMOS, told a news briefing.

"...We are seeing a flattening of the growth rate, coming to a level that is similar in other countries in this region," he added. MIMOS and national phone company Telekom Malaysia Bhd are the country's two sole Internet service providers.
The survey was the institute's its second since an initial study was done six months ago.
Mohamed said the latest survey, conducted in May to June 1997, found that 24 percent of respondents were concerned about phone charges.
Six months ago, that figure was just eight percent, he noted. "We think this is one of the main reasons for slowing down of the (usage)," Mohamed said.
Telekom began introducing timed local phone calls last year, a change from a flat rate structure.

Currently, local calls cost from one Malaysian cent to three cents per minute, compared with a previous 13 cent flat rate per call, raising phone bills for many Internet users who may be logged on for hours.
Malaysia, with a population of 21 million, has approximately 100,000 Internet subscribers. A total of 1,500 online users were surveyed.

The average Internet user in Malaysia is between 25 to 35 years old, male, married, educated and affluent, the survey found. Over 80 percent of those surveyed use modem speeds of 28.8 or above, a relatively advanced baud rate for the region, and faster than some countries like Australia.
A higher modem speed increases the efficiency of transmitting and receiving data over phone lines and cuts down the time needed to download information.
But main uses for the Internet in Malaysia are comparatively pedestrian.

Whereas many online surfers in Australia and Singapore go to cyberspace for entertainment and interaction, e-mail is the biggest activity for Malaysian Internet users, at 23 percent of those surveyed.

That was followed by news and reference (17 percent), research (15 percent) and entertainment (seven percent). Education and business uses fell in the five to seven percent ranges, said Ramin Marzbani, chairman of company www.research, that conducted the survey.
In contrast, entertainment is a primary activity for about 30 percent of Internet users in Australia and Singapore.
And unlike some Western countries which have sought to legislate against indecent material in cyberspace, Malaysian Internet users were not worried about it, Ramin said.
"Only about 1-1/2 to two percent cited indecent material as a concern with the Internet," Ramin observed. "That's quite low, it's about on par with junk mail."
